advances: For an actual three-cap planar circuit in the fixed descendant-gap regime, this gives the exact pair-or-triple mixed-area-excess threshold for retaining more than the gap level.  It refines the copositivity interface of accepted fact `2021348e0b2d8c9f`: after the three pairwise two-cap thresholds have been checked, one explicit genuinely three-cap scalar is the only remaining obstruction.  Thus any use of the boundary-metronoid and common-body geometry from accepted fact `6974f69acff32c8c` has a precise quantitative target, rather than an unspecified request for positive excess.
author: research-agent
proof:
Accepted fact `2021348e0b2d8c9f` gives (1), (2), and
\[
 M_{ii}
 =\sum_{z\in Z_\cap}\operatorname{area}(K_{i,z}).
\tag{13}
\]
The right side is at most the full cap mass \(W(A_i)\).  Every \(A_i\) belongs to the descendant collection used in accepted fact `6974f69acff32c8c`, so (3) gives
\[
 \mu_i=M_{ii}\le W(A_i)\le R_{\mathrm{desc}}(C)\le H.
\tag{14}
\]
This proves \(\delta_i\ge0\).  The planar Brunn--Minkowski consequence in accepted fact `2021348e0b2d8c9f` gives (5).

By (2) and density of \(\Delta_3^\circ\) in the closed simplex \(\Delta_3\), (8) holds if and only if there is a nonzero vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^3\) with
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}\mathbf A x<0.
\tag{15}
\]
Indeed, normalize such a vector by \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x\); if it has a zero coordinate, strictness in (15) persists after a sufficiently small perturbation toward the simplex interior.  Thus assertions 1 and 2 are equivalent.

We prove and apply the exact three-by-three copositivity criterion.  Let
\[
 \mathbf Q=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 d_1&a_{12}&a_{13}\\
 a_{12}&d_2&a_{23}\\
 a_{13}&a_{23}&d_3
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad d_i\ge0,
\tag{16}
\]
and put
\[
 b_{ij}:=a_{ij}+\sqrt{d_id_j}.
\tag{17}
\]
We claim that \(\mathbf Q\) is copositive if and only if
\[
 b_{12},b_{13},b_{23}\ge0
\tag{18}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
 0\le {}&
 \sqrt{d_1d_2d_3}
 +a_{12}\sqrt{d_3}
 +a_{13}\sqrt{d_2}
 +a_{23}\sqrt{d_1}
 +\sqrt{2b_{12}b_{13}b_{23}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]

First suppose \(d_1d_2d_3>0\).  Positive diagonal rescaling reduces (16) to a matrix with diagonal entries one and off-diagonal entries
\[
 c_{ij}:=\frac{a_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_id_j}}.
\tag{20}
\]
Restriction to the \(ij\)-coordinate plane is copositive exactly when
\(c_{ij}\ge-1\), which is (18).  On the simplex
\(x_1+x_2+x_3=1\), set
\[
 p:=1-c_{12},
 \qquad q:=1-c_{13},
 \qquad r:=1-c_{23}.
\tag{21}
\]
The quadratic form of the rescaled matrix is
\[
 1-2F(x),
 \qquad
 F(x):=p x_1x_2+q x_1x_3+r x_2x_3.
\tag{22}
\]
The pair conditions say \(p,q,r\le2\).  Every boundary value of \(F\) is at most \(1/2\).  Moreover, if
\(p+q+r\le4\), then \(F\le1/2\) throughout the simplex: among the three nonnegative products \(x_1x_2,x_1x_3,x_2x_3\), the sum of the two largest is at most \(1/4\), and maximizing a linear expression in \((p,q,r)\) subject to \(p,q,r\le2\) and \(p+q+r\le4\) puts coefficient two on at most those two largest products.

Consequently, a value \(F>1/2\) can occur only when
\[
 p+q+r>4.
\tag{23}
\]
Under (23) and \(p,q,r\le2\), all three numbers are positive and satisfy the strict triangle inequalities.  Put
\[
 D:=2(pq+pr+qr)-(p^2+q^2+r^2)>0
\tag{24}
\]
and
\[
 x_1:=\frac{r(p+q-r)}D,
 \quad
 x_2:=\frac{q(p+r-q)}D,
 \quad
 x_3:=\frac{p(q+r-p)}D.
\tag{25}
\]
These coordinates are strictly positive and sum to one.  Direct substitution, or the Lagrange equations for \(F\), gives
\[
 F(x)=\frac{pqr}{D}.
\tag{26}
\]
The identity
\[
 (p+q+r-4)^2
 -2(2-p)(2-q)(2-r)
 =2pqr-D
\tag{27}
\]
now shows that \(F(x)>1/2\) exactly when
\[
 4-(p+q+r)
 +\sqrt{2(2-p)(2-q)(2-r)}<0.
\tag{28}
\]
If a negative value of the quadratic form exists, its minimum on the simplex cannot occur on the boundary, so the same Lagrange calculation gives (25)-(26) and hence (28).  Conversely, (28) implies (23), and (25)-(27) give a strictly negative value.  Substituting (21) into (28), the rescaled matrix is copositive exactly when
\[
 1+c_{12}+c_{13}+c_{23}
 +\sqrt{2(1+c_{12})(1+c_{13})(1+c_{23})}
 \ge0.
\tag{29}
\]
Multiplication by \(\sqrt{d_1d_2d_3}\) turns (29) into (19), while the three pair conditions become (18).

It remains to check zero diagonal entries.  If, for example, \(d_1=0\), conditions (18) give \(a_{12},a_{13}\ge0\).  All terms of the quadratic form involving \(x_1\ge0\) are then nonnegative, and the remaining two-coordinate block is copositive exactly when
\[
 a_{23}+\sqrt{d_2d_3}\ge0.
\]
This is the remaining condition in (18).  In the same case, the left side of (19) equals
\[
 a_{12}\sqrt{d_3}
 +a_{13}\sqrt{d_2}
 +\sqrt{2a_{12}a_{13}
 (a_{23}+\sqrt{d_2d_3})},
\]
which is automatically nonnegative.  The cases \(d_2=0\) or \(d_3=0\), including two or three zero diagonal entries, are identical.  This proves the criterion (18)-(19) in all cases.

Apply the criterion to \(\mathbf Q=\mathbf A\).  Equations (4) and (9) give
\[
 d_i=\delta_i,
 \qquad
 a_{ij}=H-M_{ij},
 \qquad
 b_{ij}=\beta_{ij}.
\tag{30}
\]
Thus failure of a pair condition is exactly (10), equivalently (11), while, if every pair condition holds, failure of (19) is exactly \(\Xi<0\).  This proves the equivalence of assertions 2 and 3.

If a pair condition fails, the two-coordinate restriction of \(\mathbf A\) has a strictly negative value; perturbing its normalized witness into \(\Delta_3^\circ\) preserves strictness.  If all pair conditions hold, every two-coordinate restriction is copositive, so any vector satisfying (15) has all three coordinates positive.  Normalizing it gives the final assertion.  The proof is complete.
statement:
Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^2\) be a convex body, and fix an actual support-minimal balanced negative cap circuit of cardinality three in the notation of accepted facts `2021348e0b2d8c9f` and `6974f69acff32c8c`.  Write its individual caps as \(A_1,A_2,A_3\), put
\[
 K_{i,z}:=(A_i)_z,
 \qquad
 Z_\cap:=\{z:K_{i,z}\ne\varnothing\text{ for }i=1,2,3\},
\]
and let \(\mathbf M=(M_{ij})_{i,j=1}^3\) be the canonical mixed-area matrix
\[
 M_{ij}:=\sum_{z\in Z_\cap}V_2(K_{i,z},K_{j,z}).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus, for every strictly positive probability vector
\(\boldsymbol\vartheta\in\Delta_3^\circ\), the positive same-base reweighting satisfies
\[
 W(B_{\boldsymbol\vartheta})
 =\boldsymbol\vartheta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf M\boldsymbol\vartheta.
\tag{2}
\]

Put
\[
 W:=W(C),
 \qquad
 G:=\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{core}}(C),
\]
and suppose that, for some \(0<\eta\le1\), the fixed-gap hypotheses are
\[
 R_{\mathrm{desc}}(C)\le H:=(1-\eta)W,
 \qquad
 G\le\frac{\eta}{6}W.
\tag{3}
\]
For \(1\le i\le3\), define the common-support cap mass and its gap by
\[
 \mu_i:=M_{ii}
 =\sum_{z\in Z_\cap}\operatorname{area}(K_{i,z}),
 \qquad
 \delta_i:=H-\mu_i.
\tag{4}
\]
Then \(\delta_i\ge0\).  For \(i<j\), define the canonical mixed-area excess and the pair slack
\[
 \varepsilon_{ij}
 :=M_{ij}-\sqrt{\mu_i\mu_j}
 =(\mathbf E_{\mathrm{mix}})_{ij}\ge0,
\tag{5}
\]
\[
 \beta_{ij}
 :=H-M_{ij}+\sqrt{\delta_i\delta_j}
 =H-\sqrt{\mu_i\mu_j}-\varepsilon_{ij}
   +\sqrt{\delta_i\delta_j}.
\tag{6}
\]
When all three \(\beta_{ij}\) are nonnegative, put
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Xi:= {}&
 \sqrt{\delta_1\delta_2\delta_3}
 +(H-M_{12})\sqrt{\delta_3}
 +(H-M_{13})\sqrt{\delta_2}
 +(H-M_{23})\sqrt{\delta_1}\\
 &+\sqrt{2\beta_{12}\beta_{13}\beta_{23}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
Then the following are equivalent.

1. There is \(\boldsymbol\vartheta\in\Delta_3^\circ\) such that
   \[
   W(B_{\boldsymbol\vartheta})>H.
   \tag{8}
   \]

2. The symmetric matrix
   \[
   \mathbf A:=H\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-\mathbf M
   \tag{9}
   \]
   is not copositive.

3. At least one of the following mutually exhaustive alternatives holds:

   (a) for some \(i<j\),
   \[
   \beta_{ij}<0,
   \tag{10}
   \]
   equivalently,
   \[
   \varepsilon_{ij}
   >H+\sqrt{\delta_i\delta_j}-\sqrt{\mu_i\mu_j};
   \tag{11}
   \]

   (b) all three \(\beta_{ij}\) are nonnegative and
   \[
   \Xi<0.
   \tag{12}
   \]

If (10) holds, a two-cap mixture on the \(ij\)-edge already has value greater than \(H\), and it can be approximated by vectors in \(\Delta_3^\circ\) while preserving the strict inequality.  If all pair slacks are nonnegative and (12) holds, every noncopositive witness uses all three coordinates, so the witnessing probability vector is already strictly positive.  No conclusion that (10) or (12) follows from (3) alone is asserted here; deriving one of these exact inequalities from the common-body endpoint geometry is the remaining geometric step.
